Saponification. An organic chemical reaction that hydrolyzes an ester under basic conditions to yield an alcohol and the salt of a carboxylic acid. It is best known historically and commercially as the process used to manufacture soap by reacting animal fats or vegetable oils—called triglycerides—with a strong aqueous base.

The reaction proceeds via an irreversible nucleophilic acyl substitution, where hydroxide ions attack the ester carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to expel an alkoxide ion, which instantly deprotonates the resulting carboxylic acid. The reaction is driven to completion thermodynamically by the final deprotonation step, which forms a resonance-stabilized carboxylate anion that is completely unreactive toward nucleophiles.

Triglycerides—triesters of glycerol and fatty acids—are hydrolyzed to yield glycerol and three molecules of soap, which are fatty acid carboxylate salts. The reaction is characterized by the saponification value, an analytical index defined as the mass of potassium hydroxide in milligrams required to saponify one gram of fat, which is inversely proportional to the average molecular weight of the fatty acids. The soap's texture is determined by the base used, where sodium hydroxide produces hard bar soaps, and potassium hydroxide produces soft or liquid soaps.

Esters are the chemical substrates cleaved by basic hydrolysis in this reaction. Sodium hydroxide is the standard lye reagent used to produce hard soaps, and potassium hydroxide is the standard reagent used to produce soft, liquid, or shaving soaps.
